metric_rationale: This metric calculates the overall proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. In the chosen experimental design, TTB and Tallying make diametrically opposite predictions on 4 out of 6 trial types, and Tallying guesses on the remaining 2. Therefore, data generated by a TTB agent will yield a value close to 1.0 (subject to noise), whereas data generated by a Tallying agent will yield a value close to 0.167.

The experimental trials are designed such that Tallying and Take The Best (TTB) make diametrically opposite predictions on almost every trial (except one where Tallying guesses). This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with Tallying's deterministic predictions on trials where Tallying does not tie. Under Tallying, this proportion will be high (close to 1.0, subject to noise). Under TTB, since it consistently prefers the opposite option on these specific trials, this proportion will be very low (close to 0.0). The large mean difference and low variance per subject ensure a highly significant discrimination.

This metric contrasts the adherence to the Take The Best (TTB) prediction between the most 'extreme compensatory' trials and the 'non-compensatory' trials. In extreme compensatory trials, the TTB winner is opposed by a large margin of lower-validity cues (tallying margin <= -2). In non-compensatory trials, the TTB winner is supported by the lower-validity cues (tallying margin >= 1). For a pure TTB decision-maker, the number of opposing lower-validity cues is irrelevant, so adherence to the TTB winner should be roughly identical in both sets of trials, yielding a metric near 0. For a Weighted Additive (WADD) decision-maker, the large opposing margin in compensatory trials will significantly reduce the probability of choosing the TTB winner, yielding a strongly positive metric.

Under Take The Best (TTB), the choice probability is invariant to the rank of the highest discriminating cue. Thus, TTB predicts the probability of choosing Option A is the same for Trial 1 (where Cue 1 discriminates) and Trial 4 (where Cue 4 discriminates). Under Weighted Additive (WADD) theory, the probability of choosing A should decrease significantly as the validity of the favoring cue drops from Cue 1 to Cue 4. This metric computes the difference in the probability of choosing A between Trial 1 and Trial 4, which should be near 0 for TTB and strictly positive for WADD.

The experimental design systematically varies the rank of the highest valid discriminating cue (1st, 2nd, or 3rd) while controlling for the Tally difference (-1, 0, +1). According to the Strategy Mixture model, the Take The Best component is completely invariant to the absolute validity of the highest discriminating cue; it simply assigns a win to whichever option has the better value on that cue. Thus, Strategy Mixture predicts that the probability of choosing Option A will be identical across trials where Cue 1 is the discriminator vs. trials where Cue 3 is the discriminator. In contrast, the WADD model integrates validity weights, meaning the subjective advantage for Option A will shrink as the highest discriminating cue drops from Cue 1 (validity 0.95) to Cue 3 (validity 0.75). This metric directly measures the difference in choice probabilities between Cue 1 trials and Cue 3 trials. Strategy Mixture predicts a value near zero, whereas WADD predicts a strictly positive difference.

In this experimental design, every single trial features a 2-vs-2 tie in the total number of cues favoring each option. Consequently, the Tallying component of the Strategy Mixture model always predicts a 50/50 guess. The Mixture model's overall preference for the Take The Best (TTB) winner is therefore heavily dragged down by its probability of using Tallying (1 - alpha); on average across subjects, it predicts the TTB winner only about 70% of the time. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory does not probabilistically switch to a pure tallying rule. Because the highest-validity cue (0.95) is so dominant, and the subjective scaling parameter gamma is typically > 1, WADD strongly prefers the TTB winner in almost all trials, regardless of the secondary cues. By simply calculating the overall proportion of trials where the TTB winner is chosen, we cleanly and robustly discriminate the two theories. Previous attempts using zero-sum contrasts failed because WADD's preference hits a ceiling near 1.0 across all trial types, causing the contrasts to cancel out the very signal they were trying to measure.

This metric calculates the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of the choice rate from 0.5 across the six trials with highly contradictory cues and small net validity differences. Under Sequential Cue Accumulation (SCA), the evidence in these trials frequently fails to reach the threshold, triggering the 'dead zone' where the model defaults to exactly 50/50 guessing. Consequently, the empirical choice rates for SCA will tightly cluster around 0.5 (reflecting only binomial noise). Under Weighted Additive (WADD) theory, the model always integrates the cues into a graded probability that diverges from 0.5 based on the non-linear scaling of validities, leading to a systematically higher absolute deviation from 0.5.

This metric calculates the 'determinism' of choices on the most highly conflicting trials (Trials 6, 7, and 8). In these trials, the highest validity cue favors Option A, but the next highest validity cue favors Option B, and the remaining cues are distributed differently. Sequential Cue Accumulation (SCA) processes these cues sequentially. Because the cues alternate in supporting A and B, the accumulated evidence constantly fluctuates around zero and is very likely to never reach the decision threshold, causing the SCA model to default to random guessing (P = 0.5). Weighted Additive (WADD) theory, however, integrates all cues into a single compensatory score. Depending on the subjective scaling (gamma), one option will consistently outscore the other, leading to highly deterministic choices (P near 0 or 1, subject only to epsilon noise). By measuring the absolute deviation of the choice proportion from 0.5 on these specific trials, we can cleanly separate the guessing behavior of SCA from the deterministic integration of WADD, while keeping between-subject variance low.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses the option with the higher total number of positive cues on trials where the tallies are unequal (trials 1, 2, 6, and 7). In the experimental design, these trials are structured such that the option with the *fewer* total cues always possesses the single most valid cue (validity = 0.95). The advocated theory (Tallying) predicts that subjects will predominantly choose the option with the higher tally, yielding a metric value close to 1.0. In contrast, the competing WADD theory, which scales validities non-linearly (with gamma typically > 1), will overwhelmingly favor the most valid cue, thus predicting that subjects will choose the option with the lower tally, yielding a metric value close to 0.0.

This metric calculates the proportion of times Option B is chosen across Trial 1 and Trial 4. The Competing theory (Tallying with Tie-Breaking) strictly predicts Option A in both trials (Trial 1 because A has more total positive cues, and Trial 4 because despite a tally tie, Option A wins on the most valid cue). In contrast, the Advocated theory (WADD) predicts Option B in at least one of these trials for any value of gamma. For low to intermediate gamma, WADD predicts B on Trial 4 because the combined weight of the 2nd and 3rd cues outweighs the 1st and 5th. For intermediate to high gamma, WADD predicts B on Trial 1 because the 1st and 2nd cues strongly dominate the 3rd, 4th, and 5th. Thus, the mean response across these two trials will be near 0 for the Competing theory, but significantly higher for WADD.

Measures the average absolute difference in the proportion of choosing Option A between pairs of trials that have exactly the same tally difference but distinct cue validities. The Advocated theory predicts that when the tally difference exceeds a discrete threshold, decision-makers ignore validities entirely, resulting in identical choice probabilities (difference near zero). WADD continuously integrates validities, predicting distinct choice probabilities across these pairs (difference > 0).

By design, Option A always has a higher raw tally than Option B across all trials. However, in half of the pairs, Option B possesses the most valid feature (cue 0), while in the other half, Option B lacks it (and Option A has it). The Weighted Additive (WADD) theory predicts continuous sensitivity to this crucial validity difference, leading to a much higher choice rate for A when B lacks the best cue compared to when B has it. The competing Dual-Process theory posits that when the tally difference reaches a threshold, subjects switch to a simple Tallying heuristic, entirely ignoring cue validities. Because many trials will exceed this threshold, the competing theory predicts a substantially blunted difference in choice probabilities between these two sets of trials.

Trial 1 pits Option A (tally 2, but has the top two validities) against Option B (tally 3, but lower validities). The Competing Theory (Strict Tallying) will almost always choose B due to the strict tally advantage. The Advocated Theory (Dual-Process), however, uses a variable threshold. For thresholds >= 2, the tally difference of 1 is ignored, and both of its fallback strategies (TTB and WADD) strongly favor A. Thus, measuring the rate of choosing Option A on this specific trial yields a large and stable contrast between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject chooses the higher-tally option specifically on trials where the tally difference is exactly 1. The Advocated theory (Strict Tallying) rigidly predicts the subject will choose the higher tally option whenever there is any difference, so this metric should be very high (near 1.0, minus noise). The Competing theory (Dual-Process Strategy Selection) posits a threshold mechanism (from 1 to 5). On trials with a tally difference of 1, 80% of the time a subject's threshold will be strictly greater than 1, causing them to fall back to a validity-based strategy (like TTB). Because the trials are designed so the lower-tally option holds the highest validity cue, TTB users will choose the LOWER tally option. Thus, the Competing theory predicts a drastically lower score on this metric.

Focuses on Trial 8, where option A has 2 cues (the two most valid ones) and option B has 3 cues (the three least valid ones). The Competing theory strictly uses the tally difference and will robustly predict that option B is chosen (tally 3 > 2), yielding a mean response near 1.0. In contrast, the Advocated theory evaluates the configural log-odds evidence and heavily penalizes option B for missing the top two cues, making option A overwhelmingly preferred, yielding a mean response near 0.0. This stark contrast creates a massive and highly stable gap between the two theories.

Calculates the proportion of trials where the subject chose the option with the strictly higher unweighted tally, excluding trials where tallies were equal. The advocated theory (Strict Tallying) will score close to 1.0 (subject to epsilon noise) because it always prefers the higher tally. The competing theory (Configural Log-Odds) will score close to 0.0, because the experimental design specifically pits high-tally options (with low validities) against low-tally options (with high validities), causing the configural penalty and log-odds weights to overwhelmingly favor the low-tally options.

The metric calculates the proportion of times a subject chooses the option with the LOWER tally on trials where the tally difference is exactly 1. According to the Competing Theory, subjects strictly follow the tally difference whenever it is non-zero, so they should almost never choose the lower tally option (only due to noise). However, the Advocated Theory posits a variable threshold. For subjects with a threshold of 2, a tally difference of 1 triggers a fallback to the Take-The-Best strategy. The experimental design intentionally ensures that on all trials with a tally difference of 1, the Take-The-Best winner is exactly the option with the lower tally. Thus, the Advocated Theory predicts a significantly higher rate of choosing the lower tally option on these specific trials compared to the Competing Theory.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses the option with the higher tally, specifically on trials where the tally difference is exactly 1. The advocated theory (Strict Tallying with Tie-Breaker) asserts that any non-zero tally difference strictly dictates the choice, so it predicts a value close to 1.0 on these trials (modulo noise). The competing theory (Threshold-Gated Adaptive Strategy), however, allows for a threshold of 2. When the threshold is 2, a tally difference of 1 falls below the threshold, prompting a fallback to Take-The-Best (TTB). On the specific diff=1 trials designed in this experiment, TTB favors the lower-tally option. Thus, the competing theory will predict a significantly lower rate of choosing the higher-tally option on these trials.

This metric calculates the proportion of times subjects chose the option with the higher tally on trials where the tally difference is 2 or greater. According to the advocated Threshold-Gated Adaptive Strategy, the threshold for switching to tallying is at most 2. Thus, on trials with a tally difference >= 2, the decision is strictly based on tallying, leading to a very high rate of choosing the higher tally option. In contrast, the competing WADD theory continuously weighs the cues; because the lower-tally option on these trials possesses the single most valid cue, WADD will frequently select it (especially at higher gamma values), resulting in a significantly lower proportion of higher-tally choices.

This metric isolates trials where the absolute tally difference is large (>= 2) but points in the opposite direction of the most valid cue (the Take-The-Best winner). In trials 2 and 3, tally strongly favors option B, while TTB favors option A. In trial 7, tally strongly favors option A, while TTB favors option B. Under the Threshold-Gated Competing Theory, subjects ALWAYS use the tallying heuristic when the tally difference is >= 2. Thus, they will rigidly choose B in t2 and t3, and A in t7, yielding a consistently negative metric value (Low + Low - High). Under WADD, the exponential weighting allows the highest validity cue to dominate for a substantial portion of the parameter space (when gamma is large). For these subjects, WADD mimics TTB, choosing A in t2 and t3, and B in t7, yielding a strongly positive metric value (High + High - Low). This structural divergence produces a highly significant difference in means that easily overcomes the between-subject variance.

This metric leverages a double-dissociation between the Advocated theory (Noisy Take-The-Best) and the Competing theory (WADD) across Trial 10 and Trial 5. In Trial 10 (A=[0,1,1,0,0], B=[1,0,0,1,1]), WADD strictly assigns a higher subjective value to B because the sum of weights for cues 0, 3, and 4 mathematically dominates cues 1 and 2, leading to P(A) < 0.5. Conversely, the Advocated theory favors A because the validity difference for cue 1 (0.20) strongly outweighs cue 0 (0.05), leading to P(A) > 0.5. In Trial 5 (A=[1,0,0,0,0], B=[0,1,0,0,0]), WADD strictly prefers A (weight of cue 0 > cue 1) yielding P(A) > 0.5, while the Advocated theory favors B (cue 1 diff 0.20 > cue 0 diff 0.05) yielding P(A) < 0.5. Thus, the difference P(A|Trial 10) - P(A|Trial 5) will be strongly positive for the Advocated theory and strongly negative for WADD, maximizing the contrast while canceling out subject-level response biases.

The experimental design creates a conflict between the first and second most valid cues. Under the advocated WADD theory, the exponential transformation ensures that the highest validity cue consistently outweighs the second, leading to choices that align with cue 1. In contrast, the competing Noisy Take-The-Best theory evaluates cue usage probabilistically based on validity differences. Because the difference between the first and second validities (0.98 - 0.95 = 0.03) is minuscule compared to the difference between the second and third (0.95 - 0.55 = 0.40), the competing theory predicts that subjects will frequently skip the first cue and rely on the second cue instead. Thus, measuring the proportion of choices aligned with cue 1 on conflict trials will yield a value near 1 for WADD and near 0 for Noisy TTB.

Trial 5 pits a single high-validity cue (Option A) against five lower-validity cues (Option B), resulting in a tally difference of 4 in favor of B. The Advocated theory (Two-Stage Tally-Threshold) postulates a maximum threshold of 4. Consequently, for any threshold parameter (1, 2, 3, or 4), the tally difference strictly meets or exceeds the threshold, triggering the tally heuristic which overwhelmingly favors Option B. This ensures a very low, near-zero probability of choosing Option A, with minimal variance across subjects. Conversely, the Competing theory evaluates options via an exponential transformation of validities. For moderate to high values of the `gamma` parameter, the single highest-validity cue in Option A exponentially dominates the combined weight of the five cues in Option B, leading to a strong preference for Option A. This structural divergence creates a massive, reliable gap in the predicted probability of choosing Option A specifically on Trial 5, easily discriminating the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject chooses the 'High Validity Option' (the option possessing the single most predictive cue) when it is strictly outnumbered by the competing option in terms of total positive features (tally). The Advocated WADD theory, which relies on a zero-anchored exponential transformation of validities, predicts that the single best cue will often exponentially dominate a larger tally of weaker cues, resulting in a high choice rate for the High Validity Option. In contrast, the Competing Two-Stage Tally-Threshold Theory prioritizes the tally difference first; it will only choose the High Validity Option if the tally difference happens to fall below the subject's threshold AND the subject uses a Take-The-Best fallback strategy. Consequently, the Advocated theory predicts a significantly higher mean on this metric compared to the Competing theory.

This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject chooses the option with more positive ratings on the non-predictive (0.5 validity) cues, specifically on trials where the predictive cues (the first two) are perfectly tied. The Advocated theory (Sequential Evidence Accumulation) transforms validities such that 0.5 validity cues provide exactly zero evidence, predicting a 50/50 guess rate on these trials. The Competing theory (WADD) uses an exponential transformation that assigns positive weight to 0.5 validity cues, predicting a systematic preference (>50%) for the option with more non-predictive features.

This metric contrasts confidence (choice probability) in trials where the top cue(s) strongly favor the winning option vs. trials where the top cue(s) are tied, forcing reliance on weaker cues. Sequential Evidence Accumulation (SEA) expects a large drop in choice probability because early stopping on a highly valid cue yields strong evidence, whereas early stopping on a weaker cue yields much less evidence. WADD, evaluating all cues compensatorily, is less sensitive to this tie because the remaining valid cues still add up to a decisive advantage, resulting in saturated probabilities and a minimal drop. Averaging across three such pairs stabilizes the subject-level variance, ensuring a highly significant t-test.

Measures the effect of altering lower-validity cues while keeping the top discriminating cues constant. Under the competing ECSS theory, the Tallying component is always active to some degree. For Trials 5 vs 4, the Tally advantage shifts from +1 to -1 for Option A, and for Trials 7 vs 6 it shifts from -1 to -2. This predicts a substantial positive difference in P(A). Under the advocated SEA theory, decisions are likely to terminate early upon evaluating the highly valid first or second cue, completely ignoring the lower-validity cues that differentiate these trial pairs. Consequently, SEA predicts this difference to be near zero.

This metric contrasts the macro-level sensitivity to the sheer number of opposing cues (Tally difference) across all trials. The advocated Environment-Contingent Strategy Selection theory explicitly incorporates a compensatory Tallying heuristic, which strongly penalizes Option A when the tally difference is negative. Consequently, ECSS predicts a large positive difference in choice probabilities between the High Tally pool (diffs 0, +1) and Low Tally pool (diffs -1, -2). In contrast, the competing Sequential Evidence Accumulation theory evaluates cues sequentially and stops when a threshold is met. Because Option A exclusively possesses the most valid cue across all trials, SEA frequently terminates search immediately at cue 1, rendering it largely blind to the secondary cues that define the Tally differences. Thus, SEA predicts a near-zero difference between these two large pools. By partitioning all 96 trials into two halves, this metric maximizes the theoretical gap while minimizing per-subject binomial variance.

The competing theory relies on a probability mixture of Take-The-Best (TTB) and Tallying. Since the experiment fixes the validities, this mixture probability is constant across all trials. For trials 3 and 4, the TTB winner is Option A and the Tally difference is exactly 0; thus, the competing theory strictly predicts identical choice proportions. The same logic holds for trials 5 and 7, where TTB favors A and Tally favors B by exactly 1 cue. The advocated theory, however, integrates the raw validities dynamically. It predicts that Option A is chosen more often in trial 3 than in 4 (because the secondary cue validity drops from 0.65 to 0.55), and more often in trial 7 than in 5 (because Option B's validities drop from 0.85+0.75 to 0.65+0.55). This metric sums these two contrasts, resulting in an expected value of exactly 0 for the competing theory and a large positive value for the advocated theory.

The advocated theory mixes Take-The-Best (which only looks at the first cue) and Tallying (which only looks at the sum of cues). Across the experiment, trials where A has cue 1 (trials 1 and 5) and trials where A has cue 4 (trials 4 and 8) are perfectly matched in terms of both the TTB winner (always A) and the Tally difference (0 for trials 1 & 4, -1 for trials 5 & 8). Therefore, the advocated theory strictly predicts that the choice probability for A will be identical across these sets, making their difference zero. In contrast, the competing theory evaluates the specific validities of all cues, predicting a higher choice probability for A when it is supported by the stronger cue 1 (validity 0.85) than when it is supported by the weaker cue 4 (validity 0.55).

This metric exploits a structural divergence between LCA's linear summation of validities and SPRT's sequential log-odds updating. In Trials 13 and 14, the linear sum of validities for Option A and Option B are exactly equal, and their total cue counts are also equal. Because LCA evaluates evidence by linearly summing validities (modulated by total cue count) before its non-linear transducer, it predicts a choice probability of EXACTLY 0.5 for these trials, regardless of its parameter values. SPRT, however, processes cues sequentially using log-odds. Because the most valid cue favors Option A, and the sum of the non-linear log-odds yields a net positive evidence for A (+0.731), SPRT consistently predicts a high choice probability for A (>0.5). By subtracting the choice rate of Trials 13-14 from the choice rate of Trials 1-12 (where both models strongly favor A), we get a metric that is near 0 for SPRT (since it strongly favors A in both sets) but strongly positive (~0.35) for LCA (since it drops to exactly 0.5 in the latter set). Filtering for equal total cue counts across these sets completely neutralizes the between-subject variance from LCA's configural gamma parameter, ensuring extremely tight within-theory predictions.

This metric calculates the proportion of times Option A is chosen on critical trials where Option A has the highest validity cue (cue 1) but Option B has multiple moderate validity cues (cues 2 and 3). Under the advocated SPRT theory, the massive log-odds weight of the top cue dominates the sequential accumulation process, often triggering an early decision in favor of A. Under the competing LCA theory, the configural weighting is neutralized by the design, and the linear sum of the raw validities for B's moderate cues often exceeds or matches A's single top cue, leading to a much lower rate of choosing A.

This metric isolates trials where the unweighted tally difference is exactly zero (trials 1-5). Under the competing Dual-Process Dynamic Attention Model, a zero tally difference forces the model to rely entirely on the validity-weighted sum, which is mathematically identical across these trials. Thus, the competing theory predicts a flat line (difference = 0). The advocated LCA model, however, non-linearly scales the effective evidence of each cue by the total number of supporting cues (configural weighting). By subtracting the choice probability of A in low-tally trials from high-tally trials, we expose this non-linear shift predicted exclusively by the advocated theory.

This metric calculates the overall proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option with the higher tally of positive cues. By design, in all trials, the option with the higher tally also has the higher sum of validities. The advocated Dual-Process Dynamic Attention Model structurally restricts its evidence weights (beta_tally and beta_val) to be strictly positive. Therefore, it consistently predicts that subjects will favor the option with the higher tally and validity, leading to a high expected accuracy (bounded only by the lapse rate epsilon, averaging ~87.5%). In contrast, the competing Leaky Competing Accumulator (LCA) model includes a configural weighting parameter (gamma) that is sampled from [-10.0, 10.0]. When gamma is negative, the LCA non-linearly penalizes options with more cues, causing the effective evidence for the higher-tally option to drop below the lower-tally option. Consequently, for roughly half of its parameter space, the LCA model strongly predicts that subjects will reliably choose the 'incorrect' lower-tally option. This creates a bimodal distribution of accuracy across subjects for the LCA model, dragging its expected mean accuracy down to ~50%. The massive difference in expected means (87.5% vs 50%) provides a highly robust and significant discriminator between the two theories.
